title: Dedicated capacity incident lifecycle, regression simulator, and post-incident action catalogue
creator: Aisha Raman
description: Objective: reduce mean-time-to-stabilize for dedicated capacity incidents by (1) formalizing an incident lifecycle tailored to dedicated GPU pools, (2) building a lightweight regression simulator to reproduce scaling regressions and headroom collapses, and (3) producing a prioritized post-incident action catalogue and runbook changes. Context: multiple customers saw transient throughput shortfalls on dedicated pools during a rolling autoscaler regression (2025-01 incidents). The autotune/predictive-autoscaler introduced hysteresis that prevented timely scale-ups under bursty traffic patterns; coupled with conservative reserved headroom, this led to elevated request latencies and degraded SLAs. This ticket coordinates eng + SRE + product to (a) codify the emergency play and escalation path, (b) create a deterministic simulator for repro and validation, and (c) land concrete hardening items into runtime and orchestration. Deliverables: incident lifecycle doc, regression simulator (unit + integration), updated runbook and PagerDuty escalation flow, 6 prioritized action items with owners/due-dates, test plan for release gating.
acceptance_criteria: Incident lifecycle doc (PDF/markdown) approved by SRE and Support with explicit T0/T1/T2 responsibilities
Regression simulator reproduces the 2025-01 headroom collapse scenario deterministically in CI with <5% flakiness
Runbook updated with emergency throttles, fleet-level circuit, and immediate fallback model variant mapping
At least three mitigation PRs merged: autoscaler hysteresis fix, default headroom policy increase for dedicated pools, and KV-cache eviction logging
Action catalogue contains owners and due dates for all P0/P1 items and is tracked in the Dedicated Capacity Resilience project

postmortem_summary: Summary: On 2025-01-08 several dedicated pools experienced throughput shortfalls for 18-37 minutes during a regional surge. Root cause trace points to an unintended interaction between the predictive autoscaler's smoothing window and an aggressive headroom reduction rollout. The autoscaler delayed scale-ups for some pools due to hysteresis and did not recover quickly when the surge extended; conservative headroom settings amplified the service-level impact. Mitigation included temporary headroom increases, emergency throttles for low-priority customers, and a fast rollback of the predictive tuning. Outcome: SLOs were degraded for a small set of enterprise tenants (approx. 6 customers) with medium customer-impact, no data loss. Key next steps: deterministic repro tool, autoscaler code fix, runbook changes, and more conservative default headroom for dedicated pools.

root_cause_hypotheses: Predictive-autoscaler smoothing window too large for short high-amplitude bursts => delayed scale-ups
Default dedicated headroom policy was tuned for historic steady traffic; recent tenant burstiness exceeded assumptions
KV-cache eviction thrashing caused apparent latency spikes that looked like capacity pressure and triggered conservative autoscaler behavior
Rollout of predictive-autoscaler config change lacked a synthetic surge smoke test in CI
mitigation_steps: Short-term: increase dedicated_headroom default, enable emergency throttle for low-priority tenants, and revert predictive-autoscaler rollout flags where needed
Mid-term: merge hysteresis guard and add a 'fast-path' for spike detection in the predictive-autoscaler; add guardrails that trigger immediate scale when latency crosses critical thresholds
Long-term: add a dedicated synthetic surge test in gating CI for runtime changes, integrate simulator into release pipeline, and create automated canary analysis for headroom-related changes
